sources.news_title: Putin, Xi and Trump to meet at APEC summit
sources.text:
Russian President Vladimir Putin, Chinese President Xi Jinping and US President Donald Trump have agreed to meet in Shenzhen on November 19, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov told TASS.
Peskov said the three leaders would meet separately from the main proceedings of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit.
Trump and Xi last met in Beijing in May, when their talks covered the Iran war, Persian Gulf security and trade. The closure of the Strait of Hormuz had sent energy prices higher, and US officials urged China, a major buyer of Iranian oil, to use its influence with Tehran.
In July, Trump said both Xi and Putin had pledged not to sell weapons to Iran. In early November, Iranian security chief Mohsen Rezaei visited Moscow and delivered a message from Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei to Putin. The two discussed regional security, efforts to end the war and a possible gas pipeline from Russia to Iran.
Shenzhen had already figured in reports about Trump’s plans for Asia. In August, Trump was reported to have privately discussed a possible meeting with North Korean leader Kim Jong Un during an Asia trip, with the November APEC summit in Shenzhen mentioned as a potential opportunity.

sources.news_title: Trump, Xi, Putin to Meet Nov. 19; Iran In, Ukraine Out
sources.text:
The White House has confirmed that President Donald Trump, Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin will hold the first three-way meeting among their countries' leaders next week in Shenzhen, China. Nuclear weapons and the Iran war are on the agenda, according to senior U.S. officials, and Russia's war in Ukraine is not. The Kremlin put a date on it Saturday. Spokesman Dmitry Peskov told the Russian state news agency TASS that an agreement had been reached to hold the meeting on Nov. 19, on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit, which runs Nov. 18-19.
The announcement came Friday evening, when senior U.S. officials briefed reporters and a White House assistant press secretary confirmed the plan. The officials said Trump and Putin will not hold a separate one-on-one meeting during the trip, and they described the three-way session as the start of a conversation rather than a negotiation. "We do not expect to get to any kind of agreement," one senior administration official told Reuters. Tesla and SpaceX chief executive Elon Musk will travel to China with Trump but will not attend the meeting, according to officials.
Trump reaches Shenzhen after a stop in Manila, where the White House and the Philippine government say he will attend the Association of Southeast Asian Nations summit on Nov. 16. The Philippines, which chairs ASEAN this year, has declared Nov. 16 to 18 non-working days in Metro Manila for the meetings. The Shenzhen leaders' meeting brings together the 21 members of APEC, a group that includes all three countries.
Moscow has described the meeting differently from Washington. Kremlin foreign policy aide Yuri Ushakov said Thursday, after Putin received U.S. envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner in Moscow, that Putin and Trump would continue discussing the full range of issues related to a settlement in Ukraine while in Shenzhen. Ushakov had said last month that Russia and the United States had not agreed on a separate bilateral meeting between the two presidents on the sidelines. The gap between the two accounts is the central open question of the trip: Washington says the Ukraine war is not on the table, while the Kremlin says settlement talks will go on.
Peskov also dismissed comparisons to the 1945 Yalta Conference, where the wartime Allied leaders redrew the map of postwar Europe. He said any agreements reached in Shenzhen could not be imposed on others, and he called the meeting highly significant.
The idea took shape over about ten weeks. Ushakov said on Sept. 1, after the Shanghai Cooperation Organization summit in Bishkek, that the three leaders could meet at APEC and that Putin planned to hold talks with both Xi and Trump, either separately or together. Peskov said Sept. 9 that Putin and Trump had discussed the possibility in a phone call the day before. The Wall Street Journal reported in October that Putin formally proposed the three-way format in an Oct. 9 call. Putin is due to attend an APEC leaders' summit in person for the first time since 2017, according to Bloomberg, after skipping last year's gathering in Gyeongju, South Korea, where Trump and Xi met on the sidelines.
Beijing has been more guarded. Its Foreign Ministry said on Nov. 4 that it was maintaining communication with relevant parties on a meeting of the three heads of state, and it gave no agenda or date. As of Saturday afternoon, China's Foreign Ministry had not publicly confirmed the Nov. 19 date. As host of the summit, China sets the program and could ease or complicate any three-way meeting. Peskov confirmed the discussions on Oct. 19. A Kremlin foreign policy aide said Oct. 21 that China was already working on the arrangements and would include the meeting in the APEC program if conditions were favorable.
Xi has signaled little interest in making Ukraine the subject. German President Frank-Walter Steinmeier said after meeting Xi in Beijing in late October that Xi's response suggested Ukraine would not be on the agenda in Shenzhen. Steinmeier said Xi described the conflict as a European war in which Europeans must also sit at the negotiating table.
For the administration, the draw is arms control and Iran. Trump said on Nov. 8 that he expected to sit down with both leaders in Shenzhen and that nuclear weapons and the Iran war could be on the agenda, and the White House now says he will raise both.
Trump has said he is open to it. He told reporters on Oct. 19 that he had not agreed to a trilateral meeting but would be interested, that he would want to discuss nuclear weapons and denuclearization, that trade would likely come up and that it would probably take place in China. He has said earlier this year that he wants to cut military budgets with both countries, and he has noted that China may be less willing to discuss nuclear limits because its arsenal is smaller than those of the United States and Russia. The Kremlin has framed the meeting around ending the war in Ukraine on terms favorable to Moscow, according to Russian officials.
The nuclear question has a deadline behind it. The last U.S.-Russia arms control treaty, New START, expired on Feb. 5 and left the world's two largest nuclear powers without binding limits on their strategic arsenals for the first time in more than five decades. Putin had offered to keep observing the treaty's central limits for one year, a proposal Trump declined. Trump instead called for a "new, improved and modernized" treaty and has insisted that China be part of it. Beijing has declined to join such talks. A Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesman said in 2025 that it was "neither reasonable nor realistic" to expect China to participate, and when Trump pressed for trilateral negotiations at his Sept. 24 meeting with Xi in Washington, the White House readout mentioned them while the Chinese summary of the talks did not mention arms control at all.
The Iran war has already tested how far Beijing will go. Trump visited Beijing in mid-May, his first trip to China since 2017, and the war, which began Feb. 28 with U.S. and Israeli strikes, took center stage in talks that had been expected to focus on trade. The White House said afterward that both countries agreed Iran can never have a nuclear weapon, and Trump told reporters that he and Xi felt very similar about how they want the war to end. U.S. officials have urged Beijing to do more on the blocked Strait of Hormuz.
The three leaders have met in pairs this year, but never together. Trump and Xi met in Beijing in May and again in Washington on Sept. 24, during Xi's state visit. Putin and Xi met in Beijing in May and at a regional summit in Bishkek, Kyrgyzstan, on Aug. 31. Trump and Putin last held a summit in Anchorage, Alaska, on Aug. 15, 2025.
Ukraine has said it would oppose such a meeting. Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha wrote on Oct. 19 that a trilateral meeting among Ukraine, the United States and Russia could help end the war sooner, but that a meeting among Russia, China and the United States would "do only the opposite" by encouraging Putin to continue the war. He added that inviting Putin to such a meeting would give him a stature he does not deserve. Zelensky has called repeatedly for Trump to organize a trilateral meeting that includes Putin and Ukraine, and in September asked Trump to engage Xi, whom he said has influence over Putin. Putin has declined to meet Zelensky outside Moscow, a condition Kyiv rejects.
The Ukraine track has moved since then. Delegations from Russia and Ukraine met in Abu Dhabi on Nov. 10 and 11 with Witkoff and Kushner mediating, and they agreed in principle on a large prisoner exchange without reaching a breakthrough on territory or security guarantees. Witkoff said after meeting Putin that Putin had agreed to let European representatives join the next round, a point the Kremlin did not confirm. Zelensky, speaking to reporters in Dublin after the envoys briefed him, said Europeans would be at the table.
In remarks released Saturday, Zelensky said U.S. negotiators asked in Abu Dhabi, for the first time, whether Ukraine would withdraw from Donbas in exchange for joining NATO. He said there was no concrete offer, that Ukraine would not pull back its troops, and that he could put the question to a referendum only with firm security guarantees, funding for the army and money for reconstruction. He also said he would not amend the constitution to make Ukraine neutral. Zelensky has voiced concern that the Shenzhen meeting could be used to discuss a Ukraine deal without Kyiv, and he has said Russia has struck Ukrainian energy facilities more than 310 times since the start of November.
The fighting continued as the announcement landed. Ukraine's air force said Russia launched 96 drones overnight into Saturday and that 81 were shot down or electronically suppressed. Russian authorities said a Ukrainian drone attack in the Belgorod region killed a mother, a father and their 24-month-old daughter.
The timing places the summit in the shadow of the Nov. 3 midterm elections, which changed what each leader can offer. Trump's party lost both chambers of Congress, and Democrats have said they will use their new majority to challenge his Iran war and tariffs. Analysts say that the result could change how Beijing and Moscow assess Trump's staying power.
Analysts see different winners. Danny Russel, a former senior State Department official in the Obama administration, said Putin has the most to gain and called the meeting a potential diplomatic coup. Craig Singleton of the Foundation for Defense of Democracies said it could amount to a photo opportunity that lets Putin be seen alongside the U.S. and Chinese presidents.
Beijing has its own calculations. Chinese officials have weighed the downside of a high-profile trilateral summit overshadowing China's hosting of APEC, which is intended to showcase Beijing's role in the region, according to reports. Foreign Minister Wang Yi said last year that the host city, Shenzhen, would "present a spectacular event to the world." A trilateral could also give Xi a role as mediator between Washington and Moscow. China has avoided a direct role in the Ukraine war and has not joined Western sanctions on Russia, while remaining Russia's largest trading partner and a key buyer of its energy. Putin visited Xi in Beijing in May and the two signed a series of agreements, following his meeting with Trump in Alaska in August 2025.
For Trump, the meeting would also be a chance to take up trade. A trade truce between Washington and Beijing has been in place since last fall and has been extended to January, and Xi visited the White House in September, when the two sides discussed trade and Taiwan. The prospect of putting Putin and Xi in the same room with Trump also carries risks for Washington. Brookings Institution senior fellow Robert Kagan said that Russia and China could become more aggressive over the next two years if they conclude Trump is politically weakened and "on his way out," and that Trump's main interest in China is cutting economic deals. Analysts also warn that a three-way meeting would reinforce European concerns that their security is negotiable.
Expectations for substance are low. Victor Cha of the Center for Strategic and International Studies said the administration is describing the Shenzhen stop more as a short, routine visit than a summit, and that the more substantive Trump-Xi meeting is likely to come about three weeks later, when Xi is expected in Miami for the Group of 20. One analyst said a three-way meeting would happen only if Beijing had received guarantees that it would be devoid of substance. Another said the scandal around Nvidia's former chief executive and his relationship with an alleged Chinese intelligence asset is likely to be left out of Trump's talks with Xi, since neither leader gains from raising it.
The next test comes within weeks. Trump hosts the Group of 20 leaders at his Doral golf resort near Miami on Dec. 14-15. Bloomberg reported in September that Putin was likely to attend the Shenzhen summit but skip the Miami gathering, and Ushakov said Oct. 25 that any Putin trip to the United States would depend on concrete results from the November APEC meetings.
The summit would also compete with other business. Trump had been expected to seek a meeting with North Korean leader Kim Jong Un on the trip, a prospect that now looks unlikely after Pyongyang rejected talks last week, and North Korea's foreign minister this week denounced the Group of Seven's call for denuclearization. Rights groups have urged Trump to raise the case of Hong Kong activist Joshua Wong, who was sentenced last Thursday to 10 more years in prison. Group of Seven foreign ministers said after meeting in Paris that China's increasingly assertive actions in the waters east of Taiwan threaten regional stability, and Beijing called the statement a malicious smear. China's military has sent two aircraft carriers into the Pacific, and Iran is on the agenda for leaders traveling to the region.
Three markers will show which account holds: a Chinese confirmation of the date and format, whether the three governments issue a joint statement or separate readouts, and how Moscow and Washington each describe any Ukraine discussion afterward. Kyiv and its European partners, who did not choose the format, may learn what was said only after the fact. Trump is due in Manila on Nov. 16 for the ASEAN summit, and the three-way meeting in Shenzhen is set for Thursday, Nov. 19.

sources.text:
Trump to start new nuclear talks with Russia, China next week
The leaders of the world’s three largest nuclear powers will sit down next week for a historic meeting while they are all in China for the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit.
Big picture view:
Thursday’s summit of top nuclear nations is unprecedented, but many analysts do not expect any major breakthrough to come from it. They described it as an event that is more about symbolism than substance.
What we know:
Both the White House and Kremlin have confirmed the meeting between Presidents Donald Trump, Xi Jinping, and Vladimir Putin while they attend the 21-nation APEC summit in Shenzhen. The conference was meant to be a chance for China to show off how Shenzhen grew from a small fishing village to a global tech powerhouse in just a few decades, but that opportunity may take a backseat to the nuclear talks.
What they're saying:
While knowing everything that ends up being discussed between the leaders when they finally meet is difficult to predict beforehand, a senior U.S. official told The Associated Press on the condition of anonymity that Trump will likely steer conversations away from the Ukraine war.
What they're saying:
The official does not expect any new deals to be announced and described the gathering as the "beginning of, hopefully, a conversation" on nuclear disarmament "that can be productive going forward."
RELATED: Supreme Court to review Trump’s asylum ban at southern border
By the numbers:
The U.S. and Russia are believed to have more than 5,000 nuclear warheads each, while China is suspected of having over 600, according to Pentagon estimates. While the U.S. and Russia have previously had nuclear treaties, Beijing has not signaled an interest in being part of such a pact.
The backstory:
With the expiration of the last nuclear treaty between the U.S. and Russia in February, no caps remain on the size of arsenals that the two nations can build. At the time, Trump rejected an offer by Russia to extend the treaty for two years, saying he wants "a new, improved and modernized" one that includes China.
Dig deeper:
For China, joining the meeting could present Xi with an opportunity to bring his country a greater sense of clout and prestige. To Putin, sitting down with the world’s two largest economies may look like an opportunity for him to claim Russia is on par with the other superpowers.
The Source: Information for this article was taken from The Associated Press and the White House. This story was reported from Orlando, Florida.

sources.news_title: Trump, Xi and Putin plan unprecedented joint meeting on APEC sidelines, White House and Kremlin say
sources.text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — The leaders of the United States, China and Russia plan to meet Thursday on the sidelines of next week's Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in China's tech hub of Shenzhen — an unprecedented gathering of the heads of the world's biggest nuclear powers.
While the leaders gathering for joint talks will mark a singular moment, analysts say expectations are low that the talks will lead to major breakthroughs and say they will be heavier in symbolism than substance.
Plans for the three-way summit with Donald Trump, Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin were confirmed by the White House on Friday and the Kremlin on Saturday. It comes at a complicated moment in relations between the three countries.
Trump has warmly embraced Xi after coming to a truce in their short-lived trade war last year and in spite of differences over the U.S. war with Iran and other tensions between the world's foremost economic powers.
Similarly, Trump has sought to build his relationship with Putin, even as the Russian leader has persisted in his nearly 5-year-old war with Ukraine and as Moscow has deepened its military, intelligence and diplomatic partnership with Iran.
The U.S. president has insisted that such a meeting would provide an opportunity for the three leaders to discuss the U.S. war with Iran and his goal of reaching a three-way agreement on their nuclear arms stockpiles.
Trump does plan on discussing the Iran war with Xi and Putin, but will steer away from discussing Ukraine, according to a senior U.S. official who briefed reporters on the condition of anonymity.
The last nuclear arms pact between Russia and the United States expired in February, removing caps on the two largest atomic arsenals for the first time in more than a half-century. When that treaty — known as New START — expired, Trump rejected a call by Russia to extend the two-country deal for another year and called for “a new, improved and modernized” deal that includes China.
The trilateral meeting is intended to serve as the “beginning of hopefully a conversation” on nuclear disarmament “that can be productive going forward,” said the U.S. official, who added that no agreements are expected to be announced.
But Beijing’s arsenal of more than 600 warheads, according to Pentagon estimates, is far smaller than inventories held by the U.S. and Russia, each estimated to have more than 5,000 warheads. With U.S. and Russian arsenals dwarfing its stockpile, China has shown little interest in developing a nuclear pact.
Trump administration officials acknowledge that the nuclear stockpile issue is a difficult one for Beijing to engage on, but the U.S. official characterized the meeting as the moment for China to “step up ... to the adult table” on a matter of international importance.
Beijing was least certain about the value of the summit
By agreeing to host the meeting, Xi may be calculating that the moment offers him an opportunity to flex China's growing clout and prestige.
For the Kremlin, the planned trilateral meeting is a coveted chance to posture as a superpower on par with Washington and Beijing.
“I think the key for Putin was that this was very much about signaling a desire to talk to the president and talk to Chairman Xi in a way that suggests that they’re making decisions on Ukraine, which obviously the Ukrainians and the Europeans don’t like," said Edgard Kagan, a former U.S. ambassador to Malaysia who is now at the Center for Strategic and International Studies.
The trilateral could very well overshadow the APEC summit. The summit, which is bringing 21 economies to Shenzhen, marks a big moment for China to show off its fast-growing, ultramodern coastal metropolis that transformed from a small fishing village into a global technology and economic hub in just a few decades.
More substantively, such a gathering could also muddy China's argument that a Cold War mentality in the West was a contributing factor that led to Russia’s war on Ukraine and its pointed criticism that the U.S. has undermined international institutions and treaties with how it has executed its war against Iran.
The trilateral meeting could undercut China's push to portray itself as a defender of free trade at APEC, said Hoo Tiang Boon, a professor of Chinese foreign policy at Nanyang Technological University.
“You sort of run counter to Chinese support of multilateralism,” he said.
The leaders have met in pairs plenty of times over the years
Putin and Xi are no strangers. They've fostered a close personal relationship, meeting more than 40 times since Xi became president in 2013 and addressing each other as “dear friend.”
Trump and Putin have met face-to-face on seven different occasions, most recently in Alaska in August 2025. Xi and Trump have held face-to-face talks on eight occasions, including a September state visit to Washington by Xi.
Beijing is the No. 1 trading partner for Moscow, a relationship that has strengthened since Putin sent troops into Ukraine in 2022.
As the EU and the West sought to economically isolate Russia, China increased its purchases of Russia’s energy resources and became Moscow's principal supplier of key technologies, including high-tech components for Russian weapons industries. Beijing has ignored Western demands to cut those supplies.
In the lead-up to Russia's war on Ukraine, Xi and Putin declared their countries had a “no-limits friendship." China officially has said it is neutral on the conflict, while charging that Kyiv’s Western allies played a part in provoking Russia’s military action in Ukraine.
Moscow, in turn, has repeatedly declared its support for Beijing’s policy on issues related to Taiwan.
Trump recently struck a diesel deal with Russia, waiving sanctions against Moscow and allowing for the sale of millions of tons of the fuel. The U.S. leader has blamed surging energy prices on Ukraine's attacks on Russian oil refineries. Analysts, however, say the rise in global crude prices is due mostly to the Iran war.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has expressed concern that the trilateral meeting could serve as a platform for discussing a possible Ukraine deal behind Kyiv’s back.
Planning for the summit has drawn comparisons to the Yalta Conference, the 1945 gathering at which the leaders of the U.S., Britain and the Soviet Union agreed to divide Germany and Berlin into four military occupation zones and finalized plans for establishing the United Nations.
Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov has dismissed the Yalta comparisons, noting that any potential agreements reached in Shenzhen can’t be enforced on others.
“It’s clear that a meeting between the leaders of countries such as Russia, China and the United States is extremely significant,” Peskov said. “However, let’s not forget that the vision for a global order is that no one tries to impose any particular view of global order, and it should be based entirely on mutual benefit and mutual respect.”
Wu reported from Bangkok and Isachenkov from Moscow.

sources.news_title: Trump, Xi And Putin To Meet At APEC: Nuclear Arms, Iran And Ukraine On Agenda
sources.text:
- Trump, Xi and Putin are expected to meet in Shenzhen.
- Nuclear arms reduction is expected to dominate their discussions.
- The wars in Iran and Ukraine form part of wider diplomatic concerns.
Three of the world's most powerful leaders, three nuclear-armed nations and a growing list of global conflicts will come together in China next week. US President Donald Trump, Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin are expected to meet in Shenzhen on the sidelines of the APEC summit, with nuclear weapons reduction high on the agenda. But the meeting comes at a time when Washington, Beijing and Moscow are divided over trade, security and ongoing wars.
From the Iran conflict to Russia's war in Ukraine, the discussions could touch on issues with consequences far beyond their three countries. What brings these leaders together, and can their meeting deliver more than diplomatic promises?
Why Is Trump Visiting China?
Trump is travelling to China to attend the 2026 APEC summit. The summit will be held in Shenzhen on November 18 and 19. However, the most closely watched event during his visit is expected to be his meeting with Xi and Putin.
The trilateral meeting comes amid complicated relations between Washington, Beijing and Moscow.
Relations between the US and China have been marked by trade tensions, disputes over technology and disagreements over Taiwan. Although Trump and Xi have sought to maintain dialogue, issues such as tariffs, access to advanced technology, rare earth supplies and US arms sales to Taiwan remain contentious.
Washington and Moscow, meanwhile, have held various meetings recently to reach to an agreement to end the Ukraine war.
China and Russia have developed closer strategic and economic ties in recent years. Xi and Putin have met repeatedly, with both countries seeking to strengthen their partnership amid tensions with the West.
For Trump, the meeting offers an opportunity to engage both leaders on major international security issues and push for nuclear arms reduction.
What Is APEC?
APEC was founded in 1989 in Canberra, Australia, as an informal forum with 12 members. Since then, it has grown into a major platform for economic cooperation in the Asia-Pacific region that focuses on trade, investment and economic growth.
The grouping accounts for around 62% of global GDP and nearly half of worldwide trade. Its members are called "economies" rather than countries. This allows both Hong Kong, which is governed by China, and Taiwan to participate, despite Beijing claiming the latter as its territory.
China is hosting the APEC summit for the third time. It previously hosted the event in Shanghai in 2001 and Beijing in 2014.
The members of APEC include Australia, Brunei, Canada, Chile, China, Hong Kong, Indonesia, Japan, South Korea, Malaysia, Mexico, New Zealand, Papua New Guinea, Peru, the Philippines, Russia, Singapore, Taiwan, Thailand, the United States and Vietnam. India, despite being the world's most populous country, is not a member of APEC.
The forum works through consensus, with decisions and commitments being non-binding and voluntary. This year's APEC Economic Leaders' Meeting will take place on November 18 and 19, following the annual APEC CEO Summit on November 17 and 18.
Who Will Attend The APEC Meeting?
Chinese President Xi Jinping will chair the 33rd APEC Economic Leaders' Meeting and deliver the opening remarks.
Trump and Putin are among the prominent leaders expected to attend. Other participating leaders are expected to include Philippine President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. and the heads of government of Canada, Australia, Mexico, Indonesia, Malaysia, South Korea and Vietnam.
Acer founder Stan Shih will represent Taiwan.
The APEC CEO Summit will take place on November 17 and 18, bringing together business leaders and political representatives to discuss regional economic cooperation, technology and investment.
What Will Trump, Xi And Putin Discuss?
Nuclear weapons reduction is expected to be a major topic when Trump meets Xi and Putin in Shenzhen on the sidelines of APEC. The US president wants the three countries to discuss ways to reduce their nuclear weapons.
The meeting comes after the last remaining US-Russia nuclear arms control treaty expired in February 2026. However, bringing China into any future agreement could be difficult. Beijing has previously said that the US and Russia should first reduce their much larger nuclear stockpiles.
The Iran war could also feature in Trump's discussions with the two leaders. The conflict has raised concerns over global oil supplies, shipping routes and regional security. China and Russia have both criticised US policy towards Iran.
The Ukraine war is another issue that can be discussed, given Russia's continuing military campaign and China's close ties with Moscow.
However, the White House has said Trump does not plan to discuss Ukraine during the trilateral meeting. Putin may still seek to raise the conflict in his wider diplomatic engagement with Trump. The possibility of discussions without Ukraine's participation also raises concerns in Kyiv.
The Shenzhen meeting may not produce immediate breakthroughs, given the big differences between the three powers. But bringing Trump, Xi and Putin to the same table offers a rare opportunity to address some of the world's most pressing security challenges. The outcome could shape diplomatic relations well beyond the APEC summit.

sources.news_title: Historic meeting: Trump, Xi and Putin set to meet on APEC sidelines
sources.text:
Historic meeting: Trump, Xi and Putin set to meet on APEC sidelines
BEIJING — U.S. President Donald Trump, Russian President Vladimir Putin and Chinese leader Xi Jinping are due to meet in China next week for a trilateral summit, the White House and the Kremlin confirmed on Saturday.
Trump plans to discuss a possible reduction in global nuclear arsenals during the meeting, White House sources said.
The leaders are to meet in Shenzhen on Nov. 19, according to Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov. “This meeting will take place in Shenzhen on the sidelines of the APEC summit,” Peskov was quoted as saying by the state news agency TASS.
The Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit is taking place in Shenzhen on Wednesday and Thursday.
A diplomatic trilateral meeting in this configuration is historic as there have so far only been bilateral talks between the nuclear powers.
Although Trump, Putin and Xi were present at the G20 summit in Osaka, Japan, in 2019, only bilateral meetings were held at the time.
Is a new nuclear disarmament treaty on the cards?
A U.S. official played down expectations that concrete results or an agreement would be reached during the talks on nuclear weapons, calling the meeting a first step.
In the past, Trump has repeatedly raised the prospect of a new disarmament treaty. The New START treaty, concluded between Russia and the US in 2010, expired this year. New START limited the number of strategic nuclear warheads and the number of operational launchers.
When the treaty expired in February, Trump proposed a new treaty designed to extend far into the future. He also advocated involving China in nuclear disarmament treaties. Trump also recently said the U.S. was in talks with Russia and China on nuclear disarmament.
The U.S. president caused global consternation when he announced U.S. nuclear weapons tests last year, though it later transpired that these would not involve nuclear explosions.
He said that the U.S. did not want to remain the only country that did not conduct tests. During this period, Putin had instructed his government to examine the advisability of possible nuclear weapons tests.
How much of the agenda will the war in Ukraine take up?
Xi last visited Trump at the White House in September. This will be the first time the U.S. president has met Putin in person since the two held a bilateral summit in Alaska in mid-2025.
Putin last traveled to Beijing in May to visit Xi, days after Xi received Trump there.
Trump and Putin are meeting in China following the recent resumption of diplomatic talks aimed at ending Moscow’s war on Ukraine.
Russian and Ukrainian teams met in Abu Dhabi this week for talks for the first time in more than eight months, under Washington’s mediation.
Trump has long sought to encourage Xi to work with the U.S. towards ending the conflict, launched by the Kremlin in 2022. China is a key Russian trading partner. Oil imports from Russia bring in vast sums fueling the war effort. Beijing is regarded as a key source of support for Moscow on the international stage.

sources.news_title: Trump to hold trilateral summit with Xi, Putin in China next week – media
sources.text:
U.S. President Donald Trump will hold a summit next Thursday with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin on nuclear arms control, according to The New York Post.
"One of the meetings, I think, will be with President Putin and President Xi, and that'll be interesting. We'll talk a lot of things, including denuclearization, but we'll be talking a lot of things," the publication quotes Trump as telling reporters.
According to The Post, the meeting will take place on the sidelines of the APEC summit in Shenzhen. This will be the first-ever trilateral meeting between the leaders of the three countries. A White House spokesperson told the publication that issues related to Iran and North Korea may also be discussed.
The publication notes that Ukraine is not the main topic on the agenda, but the summit will take place against the backdrop of Trump's efforts to reach a peace agreement. Trump has not met with Putin in person since the summit in Alaska last August.

Trump, Xi, Putin Set to Meet for First Time for Nuke Talks
|                                                       By                             Jenn Gidman                                 withNewser.AI                                                                                   Posted Nov 14, 2026  6:22 AM CST                                                       | 
The leaders of the world's three biggest nuclear powers are set to sit down together in a first-of-its-kind meeting next week in China, US officials say. The trilateral session with US President Trump, China's Xi Jinping, and Russia's Vladimir Putin will take place on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in Shenzhen and center on denuclearization, though Washington doesn't expect concrete deals to come out of it, per ABC News.

The White House confirmed on November 13 that the three leaders will meet on November 19 on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit in Shenzhen, southeastern China. Trump and Putin will not hold a separate one-on-one meeting during the visit.
White House spokeswoman Olivia Wales said Trump intended to discuss reducing nuclear weapons worldwide, describing their proliferation as particularly dangerous. Senior US officials cautioned that no agreement was expected, characterizing the gathering as an initial conversation to open discussions on arms control.
Iran In Focus
The planned trilateral discussion comes as the Trump administration maintains economic pressure on Tehran and threatens further military action, while Russia and China retain close ties with the Iranian government.
A senior US official confirmed that Trump intends to raise Iran at the trilateral meeting but offered no details about whether Washington would seek Moscow's and Beijing's help in ending the conflict or restraining Tehran's regional activities.
Mark Katz, professor emeritus at George Mason University and a nonresident senior fellow at the Atlantic Council, told RFE/RL that Trump might hope to persuade Putin and Xi to pressure Iran to halt attacks by Tehran and the Houthis, Iranian-backed militants that control much of northern Yemen.
But Katz questioned whether either leader would cooperate. "I don't think that Putin or Xi will be willing to pressure Iran at all," he said, arguing that Iranian activities divert American attention from countering Russian and Chinese interests.
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio reinforced Washington's position at the Federalist Society's National Lawyers Convention in Washington on November 13.
Asked what would constitute an American victory in Iran, Rubio said that "Victory means [Iran] can't have a nuclear weapon. One way or another."
Rubio accused Iran's clerical leadership of pursuing an expansionist ideological agenda, sponsoring terrorism and supporting armed groups across the Middle East, including Hezbollah in Lebanon and militias in Iraq.
He argued that Tehran's missile development and uranium enrichment had brought it closer to acquiring the capabilities needed to build a nuclear weapon, despite its denials that it seeks one.
Rubio said economic pressure had weakened the Iranian government and reduced the immediate need for further military action. But he insisted that preventing Iran from acquiring nuclear weapons remained essential.
"Nothing is half a world away anymore," he said, warning that an Iranian nuclear capability would threaten the US and its regional partners.
Nuclear Hurdles
Nuclear arms control is also expected to be discussed at the trilateral meeting.
The New START treaty, the last remaining nuclear arms control agreement between Washington and Moscow, expired in February, removing restrictions on the world's two largest nuclear arsenals for the first time in more than five decades.
Trump rejected Russia's proposal to extend the agreement for another year, instead calling for a new, modernized arrangement that would include China.
That ambition faces significant obstacles, however. Pentagon estimates put China's nuclear arsenal at more than 600 warheads, compared with more than 5,000 each in the American and Russian arsenals. Beijing has shown little interest in accepting restrictions on its considerably smaller stockpile.
"We do think it's time for China to step up to the adults' table, if you will, and have adult conversations about adult things," a senior US official told RFE/RL.
The official acknowledged the difficulty of the task, saying: "We do not expect to get to any kind of agreement." He described the gathering as "the beginning of hopefully a conversation that can be productive going forward."
Luke Coffey, a senior fellow at the Hudson Institute, told RFE/RL that the meeting offered limited practical benefits for Washington.
"In reality, this will be less of a trilateral meeting and more of a bilateral one, with the US on one side and China and Russia on the other, albeit with Moscow as the junior partner," Coffey said.
He added that he could not envisage anything substantive emerging beyond giving Beijing and Moscow geopolitical validation.
Katz was similarly skeptical. "Personally, I expect no meaningful agreement emanating from the trilateral summit," he told RFE/RL. "It will mainly provide a photo op for each of the three leaders."
Ukraine Excluded
The decision to leave Ukraine off the agenda comes as Washington pursues separate diplomatic contacts with Moscow over Russia's nearly five-year-old invasion.
A senior US official said the administration had a "whole other track" for discussions about the war, involving Washington, Moscow, and Kyiv, and that China was not part of it.
"We've had many meetings recently with the Russians, but China is not really a part of that track, so it doesn't seem appropriate to have the Ukraine discussion there," the official said.
Billionaire Elon Musk is expected to accompany Trump during portions of the trip to Shenzhen because of his extensive business interests in China. Officials said Musk would not participate in the formal meeting with Xi or the trilateral summit.
His involvement comes amid growing congressional scrutiny of the role of Musk's SpaceX in Ukraine's wartime communications.
Democratic senators Jeanne Shaheen and Chris Coons have demanded that Musk and SpaceX preserve documents concerning disruptions to Ukraine's access to Starlink and Starshield satellite services in October and again on November 12.
In a November 13 letter to Musk, the senators said the interruptions had affected communications used by Ukrainian forces, including systems supporting interceptor drones defending civilian population centers against Russian attacks.
They also questioned conflicting explanations from Musk and senior administration officials about who had authority to impose the restrictions, calling for a full accounting of the decisions and greater government oversight of critical national security capabilities.
Trump's Asian tour begins in Manila, where he will attend the ASEAN summit and meet Philippine President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. before traveling to Shenzhen for APEC and his bilateral meeting with Xi.

Nuclear leaders from the U.S., China and Russia gather in Shenzhen to discuss global security
The high-stakes meeting will occur on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit in Shenzhen, marking an unprecedented moment as Washington, Beijing, and Moscow seek to address international friction.
Central to the dialogue is the status of global atomic arsenals, following the expiration of the New Strategic Arms Reduction Treaty (New START) nine months ago.
President Trump indicated that the gathering offers an opportunity for all three nations to reach a new deal on nuclear stockpiles. Aljazera also reported that "Trump plans on discussing the Iran war with Xi and Putin. "

Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov echoed a similar perspective on the meeting's scope, clarifying to Al Jazeera that “any agreements reached in Shenzhen cannot be imposed on others,” while still describing the gathering as “extremely significant”.
Beyond nuclear arms control, the three leaders plan to discuss the war in Iran, although American officials noted that the meeting will refrain from addressing Russia's war in Ukraine.

In East Africa, Kenya has experienced a sharp 26.4% drop in second-quarter exports to Middle Eastern buyers as maritime routes are diverted around the Cape of Good Hope, leading to higher freight rates and war-risk insurance surcharges.
East Africa Tea Trade Association Managing Director George Omuga told the Nation that the tea industry was “losing about $8mn a week” as millions of kilograms of tea remained stranded at Mombasa ports.
Kenya National Bureau of Statistics revealed that "exports to the Middle East fell 26.4% year on year to KES31.09bn ($241mn) in the second quarter from KES42.23bn, a drop of KES11.14bn ($86mn)"

Although crude oil exports generate over 90% of Angola's foreign sales, the nation remains heavily reliant on imported refined fuel, driving its annual fuel subsidy bill to an estimated $4.1 to $4.2 billion.

sources.news_title: Trump, Putin and Xi to hold major talks - what it could mean for Europe and Iran
sources.text:
Donald Trump has never been shy in expressing his belief in great power diplomacy.
The US President’s distrust of global alliance structures and approach to trade hark back to an era when “might is right” was the dominant philosophy among world leaders.
Friday’s confirmation of a three-way meeting between Trump, Vladimir Putin and Xi Jinping, therefore, was unsurprising, not only because US and Russian officials had been openly discussing the prospect for weeks.
However, the talks nonetheless represent a major diplomatic coup for Putin and could mark a significant shift in the security of Europe and the Middle East.
What will the talks involve and when will they be?
According to the White House, Trump, Putin and Xi will meet on the sidelines of the upcoming Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit in the Chinese city of Shenzhen.
No date has yet been set for the meeting.
Trump had already been expected to hold talks with Xi during the leaders’ summit, which will take place between 18 and 19 November, the third such meeting between the pair this year.
The President, though, also expressed interest in including Putin, both to discuss nuclear arms control and in an apparent effort to find a solution to the Iran war and soaring fuel prices.
Chinese officials were initially unconvinced by Trump’s plan, with Beijing concerned a trilateral summit would overshadow APEC and Xi’s desire to showcase Shenzhen as a growing tech-hub.
However, Mao Ning, a spokesperson for China’s Foreign Ministry, confirmed last week that negotiations over the talks were progressing with officials “in communication with relevant parties regarding a meeting between the three heads of state”.
For Xi, the three-way summit offers an opportunity to cement China’s growing clout on the world stage, as well as to play a role in addressing major international challenges.
It also presents the possibility of further swaying Trump’s approach to key issues in its favour, backed by support from Putin.
This includes the future oversight and regulation of nuclear weapons, a talking point the US President is expected to raise.
Following the expiration of the last nuclear pact – New START – between the US and Russia in February, Trump rejected the Kremlin’s offer of an extension in favour of negotiating a “new, improved and modernised” arrangement which also included China.
Trump is also keen to push Putin and Xi to exert greater pressure on Iran as part of his effort to manufacture an end to the war he began in February.
Russia and China are two of Iran’s closest allies and both have continued to provide military and economic support to the regime in Tehran throughout the conflict.
Why is Europe nervous about the talks?
European officials have expressed caution over the talks, hinting at fears Putin could use them to influence Trump’s approach to the war in Ukraine and continental security more broadly.
US media, citing an anonymous official briefed on the meeting, have reported Trump is keen to avoid discussing Ukraine, even as Russian media has talked up the prospect of the three leaders finding a solution to the conflict.
The prospect of Putin, Trump and Xi unilaterally re-writing Europe’s security framework has raised alarm in Ukraine and elsewhere.
Ukrainian officials were quick to warn the talks risked becoming “Yalta 2.0” in reference to the infamous carving up of Europe by the UK, US and Soviet Union in the wake of World War II (WWII).
Poland’s Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Foreign Affairs took to social media to echo that comparison.
“The original Yalta agreement acknowledged Soviet dominance over those parts of Eastern Europe that the Red Army controlled,” Radosław Sikorski wrote.
“Now, Putin wants to be gifted Ukrainian territories that he is unable to conquer.”
However, some experts have downplayed the comparisons.
Writing for the Lowy Institute, Alicja Bachulska, a policy fellow at the European Council on Foreign Relations, argued a repeat of Yalta was “impossible” because the US, Russia and China “do not share the same strategic calculus in trying to carve out their spheres of influence under current geopolitical conditions”.
In addition to the agency demonstrated by Ukraine, Bachulska also noted Beijing’s desire to maintain the appearance of opposing what it calls “zero-sum games” and the bullying of smaller nations by larger ones.
“In this context, [the] optics of such a meeting – even if a photo-op is the only result – might backfire against China, and Beijing seems to be aware of this risk,” she wrote.
In what European leaders may view as a positive sign, Russia has also moderated its own stance.
In response to questions from reporters about Yalta comparisons, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said the meeting between Trump, Putin and Xi was “extremely significant” before downplaying any similarities with the post-WWII talks.
“Let’s not forget that the vision for a global order is that no one tries to impose any particular view of global order, and it should be based entirely on mutual benefit and mutual respect,” he said.
Could summit lead to a breakthrough in Iran?
Unlike the war in Ukraine, Trump is keen to discuss the ongoing conflict in the Middle East with Putin and Xi.
Soaring fuel prices, driven up by Iran’s chokehold on the Strait of Hormuz, have proven economically and politically painful for the US President, who acknowledged the conflict played a role in Republicans’ historic midterm election loses.
As key allies to Iran, Russia and China have the ability to exert significant pressure on the regime in Tehran and could help force the country back to the negotiating table.
Iranian officials have already hinted that Russia is willing and able to act as a mediator in talks with the US, as has Putin.
However, the Kremlin has continued to supply Iran with weapons and dual-use technology in recent months, suggesting any intervention in negotiations would likely favour the regime.
Meanwhile, China has done little to suggest it will scale back its deep economic ties with Iran, continuing to purchase Iranian oil despite the threat of US retaliation.
Beijing has also declined to assist with a fresh sanctions push unveiled by the US, which officials said was aimed at all but collapsing Iran’s economy.
With Trump set to become a “lame duck” president for his remaining two years in office, it is unclear what incentives he could offer Putin and Xi to shift their positions.

Topics during the first ever three-way talks involving the leaders on Thursday will include nuclear arms reduction, but the U.S. side does not expect any kind of agreement, the officials added.

Huang resigned this week as chief executive of the U.S. company whose chips have powered the artificial intelligence boom, following reports of extramarital affairs with the Chinese woman and a company executive.
Meanwhile, there is no plan for Trump to meet one-on-one with Putin during his Asia trip, according to the officials. Russia is a member of the APEC grouping along with 20 other economies, including China, Japan and the United States.
Trump's entourage will include tech billionaire Elon Musk when he visits China, the officials said.

While the leaders gathering for joint talks will mark a singular moment, analysts say expectations are low that the talks will lead to major breakthroughs, and they will be heavier in symbolism than substance. AI-generated summary, reviewed by editors
It comes at a complicated moment in relations between the three countries. Trump has warmly embraced Xi after coming to a truce in their short-lived trade war last year and in spite of differences over the US war with Iran and other tensions between the world's foremost economic powers.
Similarly, Trump has sought to build his relationship with Putin, even as the Russian leader has persisted in his nearly five-year-old war with Ukraine and as Moscow has deepened its military, intelligence and diplomatic partnership with Iran. The US president has insisted that such a meeting would provide an opportunity for the three leaders to discuss the US war with Iran and his goal of reaching a three-way agreement on their nuclear arms stockpiles.
The last nuclear arms pact between Russia and the United States expired in February, removing caps on the two largest atomic arsenals for the first time in more than a half-century. When that treaty -- known as New START -- expired, Trump rejected a call by Russia to extend the two-country deal for another year and called for "a new, improved and modernised" deal that includes China.
But Beijing's arsenal of more than 600 warheads, according to Pentagon estimates, is far smaller than inventories held by the US and Russia, each estimated to have more than 5,000 warheads. With US and Russian arsenals dwarfing its stockpile, China has shown little interest in developing a nuclear pact.
Beijing was least certain about the value of the summit
By agreeing to host the meeting, Xi may be calculating that the moment offers him an opportunity to flex China's growing clout and prestige. "I would be shocked if there were a joint statement that came out of this meeting that said anything about denuclearisation," said Edgard Kagan, a former US ambassador to Malaysia who is now at the Centre for Strategic and International Studies.
For the Kremlin, the planned trilateral meeting is a coveted chance to posture as a superpower on par with Washington and Beijing. "I think the key for Putin was that this was very much about signalling a desire to talk to the president and talk to Chairman Xi in a way that suggests that they're making decisions on Ukraine, which obviously the Ukrainians and the Europeans don't like," Kagan said. sources.news_title: Trump, Xi and Putin plan unprecedented joint meeting on sidelines of APEC in China: officials
sources.text:
The leaders of the United States, China and Russia plan to meet on November 19, 2026, on the sidelines of next week's Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in China's tech hub of Shenzhen, an unprecedented gathering of the heads of the world's biggest nuclear powers.
While the leaders gathering for joint talks will mark a singular moment, analysts say expectations are low that the talks will lead to major breakthroughs, and they will be heavier in symbolism than substance.
Plans for the three-way summit with Donald Trump, Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin were confirmed on Friday (November 13, 2026) by the White House. It comes at a complicated moment in relations between the three countries.
Mr. Trump has warmly embraced Mr. Xi after coming to a truce in their short-lived trade war last year and in spite of differences over the U.S. war with Iran and other tensions between the world's foremost economic powers.
Similarly, Mr. Trump has sought to build his relationship with Mr. Putin, even as the Russian leader has persisted in his nearly five-year-old war with Ukraine and as Moscow has deepened its military, intelligence and diplomatic partnership with Iran.
The U.S. President has insisted that such a meeting would provide an opportunity for the three leaders to discuss the U.S. war with Iran and his goal of reaching a three-way agreement on their nuclear arms stockpiles.
The last nuclear arms pact between Russia and the United States expired in February, removing caps on the two largest atomic arsenals for the first time in more than a half-century. When that treaty — known as New START — expired, Mr. Trump rejected a call by Russia to extend the two-country deal for another year and called for “a new, improved and modernised” deal that includes China.
But Beijing's arsenal of more than 600 warheads, according to Pentagon estimates, is far smaller than inventories held by the U.S. and Russia, each estimated to have more than 5,000 warheads. With U.S. and Russian arsenals dwarfing its stockpile, China has shown little interest in developing a nuclear pact.
Beijing was least certain about the value of the summit
By agreeing to host the meeting, Mr. Xi may be calculating that the moment offers him an opportunity to flex China's growing clout and prestige. “I would be shocked if there were a joint statement that came out of this meeting that said anything about denuclearisation,” said Edgard Kagan, a former U.S. ambassador to Malaysia who is now at the Centre for Strategic and International Studies.
For the Kremlin, the planned trilateral meeting is a coveted chance to posture as a superpower on par with Washington and Beijing.
“I think the key for Putin was that this was very much about signalling a desire to talk to the president and talk to Chairman Xi in a way that suggests that they're making decisions on Ukraine, which obviously the Ukrainians and the Europeans don't like," Mr. Kagan said.
The trilateral could very well overshadow the APEC summit. The summit, which is bringing 21 economies to Shenzhen, marks a big moment for China to show off its fast-growing, ultramodern coastal metropolis that transformed from a small fishing village into a global technology and economic hub in just a few decades.
More substantively, such a gathering could also muddy China's argument that a Cold War mentality in the West was a contributing factor that led to Russia's war on Ukraine and its pointed criticism that the U.S. has undermined international institutions and treaties with how it has executed its war against Iran.
The trilateral meeting could undercut China's push to portray itself as a defender of free trade at APEC, said Hoo Tiang Boon, a professor of Chinese foreign policy at Nanyang Technological University. “You sort of run counter to Chinese support of multilateralism,” he said.
The leaders have met in pairs plenty of times over the years
Mr. Putin and Mr. Xi are no strangers. They've fostered a close personal relationship, meeting more than 40 times since Xi became president in 2013 and addressing each other as “dear friend.”
Mr. Trump and Mr.Putin have met face-to-face on seven different occasions, most recently in Alaska in August 2025. Mr. Xi and Mr. Trump have held face-to-face talks on eight occasions, including a September state visit to Washington by Mr. Xi.
Beijing is the Number one trading partner for Moscow, a relationship that has strengthened since Putin sent troops into Ukraine in 2022.
As the EU and the West sought to economically isolate Russia, China increased its purchases of Russia's energy resources and became Moscow's principal supplier of key technologies, including high-tech components for Russian weapons industries. Beijing has ignored Western demands to cut those supplies.
In the lead-up to Russia's war on Ukraine, Mr. Xi and Mr. Putin declared their countries had a “no-limits friendship." China officially has said it is neutral on the conflict, while charging that Kyiv's Western allies played a part in provoking Russia's military action in Ukraine.
Moscow, in turn, has repeatedly declared its support for Beijing's policy on issues related to Taiwan.
Mr. Trump recently struck a diesel deal with Russia, waiving sanctions against Moscow and allowing for the sale of millions of tons of the fuel. sources.news_title: White House confirms Trump-Xi-Putin trilateral summit in China, Iran and nuclear arms on agenda
sources.text:
The White House confirmed to The Jerusalem Post that US President Donald Trump will hold a trilateral summit with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin during his upcoming visit to China, with the war in Iran and the possibility of reducing the three countries' nuclear arsenals among the issues on the agenda.
The meeting will take place toward the end of Trump's visit to Shenzhen, following his scheduled bilateral meeting and working lunch with Xi on Thursday afternoon, November 19. The White House did not specify the exact date or time of the trilateral summit.
"The President has made it clear that, among other topics, he will discuss the reduction of nuclear weapons in the world, whose proliferation President Trump believes is very dangerous," White House Assistant Press Secretary Olivia Wales added.
During a briefing that the Post attended, senior US officials cautioned that the administration does not expect the first meeting to produce a nuclear arms control agreement but that it may begin the process.
"We do not expect to get to any kind of agreement," a senior US official said, describing the summit as "the entry point, the first conversation."
The Kremlin confirmed on Saturday that President Vladimir Putin would meet with Trump and Xi on the sidelines of the APEC summit in China on November 19.
Time for China to have 'adult conversations,' White House official says
While Washington and Moscow have decades of experience negotiating arms control agreements, the official suggested that Beijing could prove a more difficult participant.
"We do think it's time for China to sort of step up, you know, to the adults' table, if you will, and have adult conversations about adult things," the official said.
The official accused China of developing its nuclear arsenal without sufficient transparency, arguing that decisions made in Beijing have implications for international security.
Iran on the agenda, Ukraine excluded
One of the most significant revelations during the briefing concerned the wars in Iran and Ukraine.
A senior US official confirmed that Trump intends to raise the war in Iran during his meeting with Xi and Putin, but does not plan to discuss the war in Ukraine in the same forum.
"I think the president does intend to talk about Iran in the trilateral meeting," the official said.
The official offered no details about what Trump intends to propose to the Russian and Chinese leaders regarding Iran, or whether Washington will seek their support for a new diplomatic initiative to end the conflict.
On Ukraine, however, the administration drew a clear distinction.
"We have a whole nother track that you're aware of, where we've had many meetings recently with the Russians," the official explained, adding that "China is not really a part of that track."
The official also clarified that there is no separate bilateral meeting scheduled between Trump and Putin during the visit.
The decision to include Iran in the three-way discussions comes amid renewed uncertainty over Washington's approach to Tehran.
Trump said earlier this week that the United States no longer needed an agreement with Iran, while directing Vice President JD Vance, who had been involved in diplomatic contacts concerning the conflict, to focus his attention on domestic corruption investigations.
The president has continued to threaten additional military action against the Iranian regime, even as his administration has emphasized the economic pressure being exerted on Tehran.
The upcoming summit indicates that the administration intends to keep Iran on the diplomatic agenda with Moscow and Beijing, both of which maintain ties with Tehran.
Nevertheless, officials did not elaborate on what role, if any, Russia or China might be asked to play in ending the war.
Trump to meet Xi on Thursday afternoon
Wales also provided the Post and other reporters with a detailed itinerary for Trump's trip, which begins early Monday morning, November 16.
Trump is set to meet with leaders of the Quad – the United States, Japan, India and Australia – to discuss security, prosperity and cooperation across the Indo-Pacific, in Manila on Tuesday evening as well as participate in a special US-ASEAN summit.
Trump will then meet with the Philippine president at the presidential palace in order to meet regarding commercial agreements and strategic investments intended to strengthen US interests in aviation, defense, energy and technology
On Thursday morning, November 19, the president will participate in a multilateral meeting with APEC leaders before holding a bilateral meeting with Xi.
The meeting follows two previous encounters between the leaders this year: Trump's May visit to Beijing and Xi's September visit to Washington.
According to Wales, the administration intends to build on economic and trade commitments reached during those meetings.
The trilateral summit with Putin is scheduled to take place at the conclusion of the China visit.
Elon Musk to accompany Trump for part of China visit
The White House also disclosed that Elon Musk, the chief executive of Tesla and SpaceX, is expected to accompany Trump during portions of his visit to China.
"We believe there will be at least one high-profile business leader," a senior US official said, identifying the executive as the head of Tesla and SpaceX.
The official said Musk's participation would be limited to certain portions of the China stop, rather than the entire presidential trip.
Asked why Musk was joining the delegation, the official cited his extensive business interests in the US-China relationship and his role in sectors relevant to American national security.
The official suggested that Musk could be valuable to the president in an advisory capacity, although he declined to speak on Trump's behalf about the precise reason for the invitation.
Musk, however, will not participate in the trilateral summit or the president's bilateral meeting with Xi.
"Those will be official meetings with officials only participating," the official said.
The official also downplayed the possibility of detailed discussions about Starlink, SpaceX's satellite communications network, and its role in the war in Ukraine.
The administration does not expect to bring a broader American business delegation on the trip.
Some US business executives are expected to attend the China-hosted APEC CEO Summit, but officials emphasized that their participation would be at China's invitation and would not make them part of the official US delegation.
Nvidia espionage scandal not expected to affect Xi talks
Senior US officials also addressed whether the unfolding scandal surrounding former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang would affect Trump's discussions with Beijing.
Huang resigned this week following revelations about extramarital relationships, including one involving a woman US intelligence officials reportedly suspect of working for Chinese intelligence, as well as reports of relationships with company employees.
The allegations have raised concerns about the potential exposure of sensitive American technology and the possible implications for US national security.
But the White House does not expect the controversy to become part of the talks with Xi.
"The situation with Nvidia should not really have any bearing on the trip," a senior US official said.
The administration is nevertheless considering measures to strengthen existing restrictions on the export of advanced American AI chips.
Rare earth minerals and trade remain major sticking points
Beyond nuclear security and regional conflicts, Trump's bilateral meeting with Xi is expected to focus heavily on the implementation of existing trade agreements.
Senior US officials told reporters, including the Post, that Washington remains frustrated with China's performance on its commitments to supply rare earth minerals and related products, which are critical to industries ranging from defense manufacturing to advanced electronics.
"We're not getting them at the pace and at the level that we would like to be receiving them at," a senior US official said.
The official explained that the administration's concerns contributed to its decision to extend the Busan agreement for only two months rather than six.
Washington wants Beijing to demonstrate more consistent compliance with its commitments.
"I expect the president will raise it with President Xi," the official said.
The administration also remains concerned about Chinese non-tariff barriers, which officials say can undermine the benefits of tariff-reduction agreements.
A senior official said American and Chinese representatives met earlier on Friday to discuss trade implementation issues.
Despite those ongoing negotiations, the White House does not expect to announce a new tariff agreement immediately after the Trump-Xi meeting.
The meeting is instead expected to review progress under existing arrangements.
Finally, officials ruled out any currently planned engagement with North Korean leader Kim Jong Un during Trump's Asian tour.
"As of right now ... there are no plans at all for engagement with North Korea," a senior US official said.
The trip will place Trump at the center of a series of major diplomatic and economic discussions across Asia. Its centerpiece, however, will be the trilateral summit with Xi and Putin – an effort to initiate a new discussion about nuclear arms control among the three powers while the war in Iran continues and their wider strategic relationships remain under strain.

Trump to raise nuclear-arms cuts with Putin, Xi on Thursday, White House says
By Trevor Hunnicutt and Jasper Ward
WASHINGTON, Nov 13 (Reuters) - US President Donald Trump will raise nuclear-arms reduction at a meeting in China next week with Russian President Vladimir Putin and Chinese President XiJinping, the White House said on Friday.
"He will discuss the reduction of nuclear weapons in the world, whose proliferation President Trump believes is very dangerous," Olivia Wales, a White House spokeswoman, said on a call with reporters. She added that the meeting would take place on Thursday in China.
Trump's repeated insistence that the first-of-its-kind meeting of the three leaders focus on nuclear arms reductions has riled China, which is hosting a summit focused on trade and commerce. China has rebuffed attempts to talk about nuclear arms with Russia and the United States, which have the largest stockpiles of such weapons.
Putin, Xi and Trump are expected to meet on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation forum in Shenzhen. Trump is leaving on Monday for a four-day trip to Asia that also includes a stop in the Philippines.
"We do not expect to get to any kind of agreement," a senior Trump administration official said regarding the nuclear issue. "This is a difficult topic for China to address, but we do think it's time for China to sort of step up, you know, to the adults' table, if you will, and have adult conversations about adult things."
The official added: "This is the beginning of hopefully a conversation that can be productive going forward."
Beijing has for years resisted direct engagement with Washington about its nuclear program, saying it is more appropriate for Russia and the US to speak directly because of their large arsenals.
Russia has the most stored nuclear warheads, followed by the United States and China, according to the Stockholm International Peace Research Institute. The New Strategic Arms Reduction Treaty between the US and Russiaexpired this year.
It was not clear whether Russia or China intended to engage in a conversation about arms reductions with Trump.
The Chinese and Russian embassies in Washington did not immediately respond to emailed requests for comment.
Trump will also raise the US-Israeli war against Iran in the meeting but is not expected to raise Russia's war in Ukraine, the official said.
The Republican president is not expected to have a one-on-one meeting with Putin or discuss Ukraine's access to satellite communications service provided by Elon Musk's SpaceX. Musk is joining Trump on the trip to China but will not attend his meeting with Xi and Putin, according to the official.
"We've had many meetings recently with the Russians, but China is not really a part of that track, so it doesn't seem appropriate to have the Ukraine discussion there," the person said.
Trump is also not expected to meet with North Korean leader Kim JongUn during his trip to Asia, according to the official.
(Reporting by Jasper Ward and Trevor Hunnicutt in Washington; Editing by Caitlin Webber)

Trump administration delays Medicaid work requirements by six months
The federal government today announced a six-month delay in enforcing a Medicaid work requirement — a central provision in Trump’s “big, beautiful bill” that experts said would lead millions of Americans to lose health coverage.
The requirement still technically starts on Jan. 1, but under new guidance from the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services, states that choose not to enforce it won’t be held accountable until at least July 1.
The move is a striking turn for an administration that has spent months defending the policy against criticism from state officials and healthcare advocates who warned that the rollout was moving too quickly and that people who should be eligible for Medicaid would lose coverage because of the additional red tape and paperwork.
CMS called the six-month window a “hold harmless” period, and the delay is optional. States that choose to take advantage of this period will still start checking on Jan. 1 whether Medicaid enrollees are working, volunteering or in school or whether they qualify for an exemption. The broadside is the latest sign of strain inside the administration since Nvidia ousted CEO Jensen Huang over an affair with a suspected Chinese spy, a scandal that rocked Washington and the tech world. Huang is close to President Donald Trump and had pushed to loosen restrictions on sales of chips to China.
The honey trap, explained: The spy tactic that has ensnared congressmen, colonels and a CEO
The U.S. government’s suspicion that Nvidia’s outgoing CEO Jensen Huang was having an affair with a woman spying for China may sound like a movie plot, but the age-old espionage tactic known as a honey trap is a very real source of anxiety within America’s tech industry.
The ploy goes by various names, including honey trap, honeypot, sexpionage and sex warfare, but the general idea is the same: The prospect of sex or romance is used as bait to gain access to or leverage over someone with inside information or influence.

He warned the crowd to remember "that the same disgust with the status quo that got Democrats elected this year is the disgust with the status quo that got Republicans elected the last time around, and that should remind us as we think about what we are getting ready to do."

The leaders of the United States, China and Russia plan to meet Thursday on the sidelines of next week’s Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in China’s tech hub of Shenzhen — an unprecedented gathering of the heads of the world’s biggest nuclear powers.
While the leaders gathering for joint talks will mark a singular moment, analysts say expectations are low that the talks will lead to major breakthroughs and say they will be heavier in symbolism than substance.
Plans for the three-way summit with Donald Trump, Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin were confirmed on Friday by the White House. It comes at a complicated moment in relations between the three countries.

Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s resignation rattles global markets
Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s sudden resignation following an admitted affair with a woman thought by intelligence officials to be a Chinese spy, is sending shockwaves through the AI industry and global financial markets. Now, some lawmakers are calling for investigations into whether U.S. security has been compromised by Huang’s actions. NBC’s Brian Cheung reports for "TODAY."
Sen. Cory Booker pushes Democrats to be 'bold doers' as they take control of Congress
Sen. Cory Booker, D-N.J., urged Democrats tonight to meet the moment as they prepare to take power of Congress in January, saying that "voters said very clearly that we want America to be America again."
"This is a moral moment in America. This is not a partisan one," Booker said at Majority Democrats’ “What’s Next” conference. "It is not left or right. It is right or wrong, and the voters told us so."
Booker told the crowd, "This is not a moment for small thinkers. This is a moment for bold doers."
"People who have jumped from one party to the next are just looking for someone that will help carry us forward," he said. "They are looking for someone that, again, will say, 'I too sing America,' a song that is inclusive, a song for everyone, a song that is our creed. We the people."

Senate Democrats to hold leadership elections on Dec. 1
Senate Democrats will hold their leadership elections on Dec. 1, according to two leadership sources.
The next majority leader needs to win over a simple majority to earn the role.

Blue wave ignites a wild, wide-open 2028 race
Last week’s Democratic midterm sweep reached so far and so wide that it is already recasting conventional thinking about who can forge a winning path to the White House in 2028 — blowing the doors off of what was already expected to be a wide-open presidential race.
There was something for everyone in Democratic politics. Moderates won, but so did progressives. Women scored victories in deep-red, statewide races. Candidates who didn’t have the most money won. Rubio says 'politics requires more than simply winning elections,' in plea to conservatives to continue fighting
Secretary of State Marco Rubio told the Federalist Society at the National Lawyer’s Convention tonight to continue their work to uplift conservative ideology, as "great things that last are built in decades, not election cycles."

Secretary of State Marco Rubio, as he delivers his first major speech since Republicans' devastating losses in the midterm elections, tonight took aim at Democratic Rep. Robert Garcia's pledge to investigate the Trump administration.

“I believe that the size and scale of these majorities provides an opportunity for the United States Senate to answer the call with the American people,” Van Hollen said, later definitively adding, "I'm not running in 2028."
