By Peter Kuznick and Ivana Nikolić Hughes, World BEYOND War, November 15, 2026
Presidents Jinping, Putin, and Trump should pursue a diplomatic breakthrough in China, with an eye on a nuclear weapons-free world.
Excitement abounds around the possible, perhaps likely, upcoming tripartite meeting in Shenzen, China among Presidents Xi Jinping, Vladimir Putin, and Donald Trump at the November 18-19 meeting of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit. Some are calling it Yalta 2.0. We’d rather think of it as Reykjavik 2.0., while also welcoming some of the broader diplomatic breakthroughs and global reordering achieved at Yalta almost 82 years ago.
Dmitry Trenin, former longtime director of the Carnegie Moscow Center and current President of the Russian International Affairs Council, wrote encouragingly, “The US president has mentioned that an unprecedented trilateral meeting…would make sense if it were focused on denuclearization.” Trenin wrote this in Al Jazeera in the context of explaining why Russia could play a helpful role in negotiating a new nuclear agreement between its Iranian ally and the United States. While anything that might help end the dangerous, destructive, and potentially apocalyptic conflagration in Southwest Asia would be more than welcome, we think the leaders can and should reach even higher. Why not rekindle the spirit of the 1986 meeting between Presidents Ronald Reagan and Mikhail Gorbachev, at which they came within a hairsbreadth, arguably one word, of eliminating not only all ballistic missiles as Reagan originally proposed but all nuclear weapons as Gorbachev countered. Reagan replied, “Yes, all” and Secretary of State George Shultz agreed. “Let’s do it,” he said. The chance to achieve the most extraordinary diplomatic breakthrough in history slipped through Reagan’s grasp when he insisted on unlimited testing of his Strategic Defense Initiative (SDI) fantasy rather than limiting SDI to the laboratory for ten years. The world’s hopes were dashed and we have not come even close ever since.
Sure, we’re up against obstacles and the odds against this are long. Donald Trump has responded to the midterm shellacking by appointing Stephen Miller as Chief of Staff—in effect giving the middle finger to those who didn’t support the Republicans, which is not a hopeful sign. Putin knows that much of Russian power comes not from its economic prowess or its conventional military but from possessing the largest nuclear arsenal in the world. And Xi Jinping has made it clear that China won’t engage in arms control talks until it achieves rough nuclear parity with the U.S. and Russia; it has been rapidly increasing the size of its arsenal as a result.
That said, there are good reasons why all three could support this proposal. After Tuesday’s humiliating trouncing, Trump, probably the most recalcitrant of the three, may be desperate for an achievement that could cement at least a piece of a positive legacy—and in this case a very big piece, a resounding piece. And he has been all over the map on the nuclear issue. In February 2025, he said, “There’s no reason for us to be building brand-new nuclear weapons. We already have so many. You could destroy the world 50 times over, 100 times over. And here we are building new nuclear weapons, and they’re building nuclear weapons.” He also said, “We’re all spending a lot of money that we could be spending on other things that are actually, hopefully, much more productive.” This is apparently something he’s been contemplating for many years. In 2016, he told the New York Times’ Maggie Haberman and David Sanger: “I personally think it’s the biggest problem the world has, nuclear capability. I think it’s the single biggest problem….Power of weaponry today is beyond anything ever thought of, or even, you know, it’s unthinkable, the power….And to me, it’s the single biggest, it’s the single biggest problem.” He credits his “very brilliant” MIT physicist uncle John Trump with making him aware of this danger.
In 1986, he sought the advice of Nobel laureate and International Physicians for the Prevention of Nuclear War founder Dr. Bernard Lown on negotiating nuclear disarmament with Gorbachev. He told Lown that he would get Reagan to send him to Moscow and he would secure disarmament and end the Cold War in one hour.” Lown commented, “I sat there dumbfounded. ‘Who is this self-inflated individual? Is he sane or what?’”
On January 23, 2025, he told the World Economic Forum in Davos: “And I will tell you that President Putin really liked the idea of — of cutting way back on nuclear. And I think the rest of the world, we would have gotten them to follow. And China would have come along too. China also liked it. Tremendous amounts of money are being spent on nuclear, and the destructive capability is something that we don’t even want to talk about today, because you don’t want to hear it. It’s too depressing. So, we want to see if we can denuclearize, and I think that’s very possible. And I can tell you that President Putin wanted to do it. He and I wanted to do it. We had a good conversation with China. They would have been involved, and that would have been an unbelievable thing for the planet.”
Whether or not Trump is sane is even more heatedly debated today than it was 40 years ago, but that Trump may be iconoclastic enough to take a dramatic step that reverses the course of history should not be. The question is whether he’s capable of taking such a step in favor of humanity rather than against it.
Similarly with Putin. Putin told a meeting of the Valdai International Discussion Club in Sochi in 2017, “Should you ask me if nuclear disarmament is possible, I will tell you ‘yes, it is possible. Does Russia wish to achieve universal nuclear disarmament or not? The answer is in the affirmative, too. Yes, it does, and it will be working for it.” Shortly before the invasion of Ukraine, the leaders of the U.S., Russia, China, France, and the United jointly declared:
“We affirm that a nuclear war cannot be won and must never be fought… we remain committed to our Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty (NPT) obligations, including our Article VI obligation to pursue negotiations in good faith on effective measures relating to cessation of the nuclear arms race at an early date and to nuclear disarmament.” Skeptics will rightly point out that this was before the invasion of Ukraine and a series of slightly veiled nuclear threats that Putin issued. But it at least offers a glimmer of hope, especially in the context of a security agreement that promises peaceful coexistence for all participants.
In 2017, in a speech at the United Nations Office in Geneva, Xi Jinping said clearly, “Nuclear weapons, the Sword of Damocles that hangs over humankind, should be completely prohibited and ultimately destroyed over time to make the world free of nuclear weapons.” While not disavowing this sentiment, Xi has more recently indicated that China would not participate in arms control discussions until it had achieved rough parity with largest nuclear powers–the United States and Russia. Fine. To most people, that means China increasing the size of its arsenal to the 5,000 plus weapons that both Russia and the United States possess. We have a different proposal. How about if the U.S. and Russia reduce their arsenals down to the 600 or so that China now possesses?
We see this being done in three four-year stages, much as Reagan and Gorbachev envisioned 40 years ago. In the first stage, the U.S. and Russia pare down their arsenals while China forgoes its expansion. During this trust-building stage, the wars in Iran and Ukraine would need to end quickly, alongside a recommitment to the UN Charter and peaceful development by not just China, Russia, and the U.S., but all nuclear armed states. The second four-year stage, would be more complex, as it would involve bilateral, trilateral, and multi-lateral negotiations among all nine nuclear armed states to address the specific reasons why each of the states possesses nuclear weapons, and to find ways that those incentives could be reduced or eliminated. Intense diplomacy would be required during this period, resulting in all nine nuclear powers joining the Treaty on the Prohibition of Nuclear Weapons (TPNW). The TPNW would give all nine states a ten-year timeline to eliminate their arsenals. However, they could accomplish this in four years, given that the starting point would be arsenals of no more than 600 nuclear warheads. This last four-year stage would involve reductions, verification, and eventual elimination of arsenals. It could be done in plenty of time for the centennial celebration of the United Nations, and the centennial commemoration of the atomic bombings of Hiroshima and Nagasaki. The nuclear age should end well before it turns 100.
If Reagan and Gorbachev could come so close 40 years ago, we should not rule out the possibility that Putin, Xi, and Trump could do so today. As John Kennedy said in his great American University Commencement Address in 1963, “Our problems are man-made—therefore, they can be solved by man. And man can be as big as he wants. No problem of human destiny is beyond human beings. Man’s reason and spirit have often solved the seemingly unsolvable—and we believe they can do it again.”

WASHINGTON, November 14, 2026 – US President Donald Trump is preparing for an unprecedented meeting with Russian President Vladimir Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping in China next week, placing nuclear arms control, the conflict involving Iran and the shifting balance of global power at the centre of an unusually high-stakes diplomatic encounter.
The three leaders are scheduled to meet on November 19 on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit in Shenzhen, according to the White House and subsequent confirmation from the Kremlin. The APEC leaders’ gathering takes place on November 18 and 19.
The White House announcement, reported by Reuters and The Associated Press, said Trump intended to raise the reduction of nuclear weapons with Putin and Xi. Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov subsequently confirmed that an agreement had been reached for the trilateral meeting.
The gathering would bring together the leaders of the United States, Russia and China, the world’s three leading nuclear powers, at a time when the international arms-control framework is under considerable strain.
However, Washington has played down expectations of an immediate breakthrough.
“We do not expect to get to any kind of agreement,” a senior US official told reporters, according to Reuters and AP. The administration views the discussion as an opportunity to begin engagement rather than conclude a comprehensive nuclear agreement.
Nuclear arms control takes centre stage
Trump’s interest in nuclear disarmament comes amid the weakening of the international framework governing the world’s largest nuclear arsenals.
The expiration of the New START treaty between Washington and Moscow in February 2026 removed the last major bilateral agreement placing limits on the strategic nuclear forces of the two countries.
The treaty had provided a framework for limiting deployed strategic nuclear warheads and delivery systems, alongside verification arrangements intended to improve transparency between the two nuclear powers.
Its expiration has intensified concerns about the absence of enforceable constraints on the world’s largest nuclear arsenals.
Trump has previously expressed interest in a broader arms-control arrangement involving China, arguing that any future framework should account for Beijing’s expanding nuclear capabilities.
That ambition faces a significant diplomatic obstacle. China has repeatedly resisted participating in trilateral nuclear negotiations, maintaining that its arsenal remains substantially smaller than those of the United States and Russia.
Beijing has argued that Washington and Moscow, which possess considerably larger stockpiles, should first make further reductions before expecting China to participate in negotiations on equal terms.
This difference in negotiating positions makes a comprehensive agreement difficult to achieve in Shenzhen. Nevertheless, bringing the three leaders into the same room could establish a political channel for future discussions.
Iran, rather than Ukraine, is expected to dominate Trump’s agenda
Although the presence of Putin will inevitably draw attention to Russia’s war against Ukraine, US officials have indicated that Trump intends to concentrate on Iran rather than the conflict in Eastern Europe.
The White House has said nuclear weapons reduction will be among the issues discussed, while a senior US official indicated that the US-Israeli war involving Iran would also feature in the discussions.
Ukraine is not expected to be a principal subject of the trilateral meeting.
Washington maintains a separate diplomatic track involving Kyiv and Moscow, and officials have suggested that the absence of Ukraine from the three-way discussion reflects the fact that China is not directly part of those negotiations.
The decision is diplomatically significant. Moscow has sought to maintain international attention on the Ukraine conflict, while Washington appears intent on keeping the Shenzhen meeting focused on issues where it believes direct engagement with Beijing and Moscow could produce progress.
For Putin, participation offers an opportunity to engage directly with the US president and reinforce Russia’s position as a major international power. For Trump, the meeting provides an opportunity to demonstrate that his administration can maintain dialogue with competing global powers while pursuing its own foreign-policy priorities.
China faces pressure over its nuclear ambitions
Xi’s participation will place China under renewed international scrutiny over the development and transparency of its nuclear capabilities.
The United States has increasingly argued that China’s expanding military capabilities make its participation in future arms-control arrangements necessary.
Beijing, however, has resisted being drawn into negotiations structured around the much larger US and Russian arsenals. Its position reflects a longstanding concern that trilateral negotiations could impose obligations disproportionate to China’s current nuclear capabilities.
The Shenzhen meeting therefore presents Xi with a delicate diplomatic calculation. China wants to preserve its strategic autonomy while avoiding the impression that it is unwilling to engage with international efforts to reduce nuclear risks.
There is also a broader geopolitical dimension. China is hosting the APEC summit at a time when trade, technology, security and regional influence remain central areas of competition with Washington.
A meeting involving Trump and Putin would give Beijing an opportunity to project itself as a central diplomatic power capable of convening the leaders of countries with competing strategic interests.
However, agreeing to attend discussions does not necessarily mean accepting the negotiating framework proposed by Washington.
A separate Trump-Xi meeting adds economic significance
Alongside the trilateral gathering, Trump is scheduled to hold separate talks with Xi on November 19.
The bilateral meeting is expected to address the wider US-China relationship, which continues to be shaped by trade disputes, technology restrictions, supply-chain security and competition over strategic industries.
The relationship has significant implications for global markets because the United States and China remain two of the world’s largest economies and major participants in international trade.
Businesses and investors will be watching for signals on tariffs, technology exports, critical minerals and the durability of the trade understanding between the two governments.
Any indication that Washington and Beijing are prepared to maintain dialogue could help reduce uncertainty for companies operating across international supply chains. Conversely, renewed disagreements could intensify concerns over trade fragmentation and the cost of doing business across the world’s two largest economic powers.
The meeting also comes as the Trump administration seeks to balance its economic competition with China against the need for cooperation on issues such as nuclear proliferation and international security.
Moscow, Beijing and Washington exchange views
Before the White House announcement, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said Moscow, Beijing and Washington were exchanging views on the agenda for a possible trilateral meeting.
His subsequent confirmation that the leaders would meet on November 19 marks a progression from preliminary diplomatic discussions to an agreed high-level encounter.
The absence of a separate Trump-Putin bilateral meeting is also notable. It suggests that Washington is prioritising the collective format rather than arranging a standalone engagement between the US and Russian presidents during the visit.
The three governments will nevertheless approach the gathering with different strategic objectives. Washington wants to bring China into discussions on nuclear arms control, Moscow wants to preserve its influence in negotiations involving the United States, and Beijing wants to avoid accepting obligations that it considers disproportionate to its nuclear capabilities.
Those competing interests will limit the scope for immediate agreement.
A historic meeting with uncertain outcomes
The Shenzhen meeting could become an important moment in international diplomacy, but its significance should not be confused with the likelihood of a major agreement.
The three leaders have different expectations of what nuclear arms control should achieve, while their governments remain divided over security, trade, military competition and the future of the international order.
A successful meeting may therefore be measured less by the signing of an agreement than by whether the leaders establish a credible basis for further negotiations.
For Trump, the challenge will be to turn an ambitious diplomatic gathering into a practical process. For Xi, it will be to demonstrate international leadership without compromising China’s strategic position. For Putin, the meeting offers an opportunity to maintain direct engagement with Washington at a time of continuing confrontation over Ukraine and wider security issues.
The immediate outcome may be limited. But bringing the leaders of the United States, Russia and China together to discuss nuclear weapons at a time when the last major US-Russia arms-control treaty has expired is, in itself, a significant diplomatic development.
The world will be watching not simply what the three presidents say in Shenzhen, but whether their meeting produces a sustained conversation capable of reducing the risks of a new nuclear arms race.

Beijing/Washington: Chinese President Xi Jinping, US President Donald Trump and Russian President Vladimir Putin are set to hold an unprecedented trilateral meeting next week on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit in China’s Shenzhen city, the White House has said.
China is set to host the 33rd APEC Economic Leaders’ Meeting November 18-19, with leaders of the 21-member grouping attending the summit.
Discussions at the trilateral meeting are expected to focus on a range of global issues, including conflicts, artificial intelligence and nuclear arms reduction.
The proposed discussion on nuclear weapons comes amid concerns over the future of global arms control following the expiry of the New START treaty between the US and Russia in February.
The last remaining major bilateral nuclear arms control agreement between the two countries, it placed legally binding limits on their strategic nuclear arsenals. Its expiry has left the world’s two largest nuclear powers without such binding limits.
“The president has made it clear that, among other topics, he will discuss the reduction of nuclear weapons in the world, whose proliferation President Trump believes is very dangerous,” BBC quoted White House spokeswoman Olivia Wales as saying.
The Hong Kong-based South China Morning Post reported that the discussions could also explore possible commitments on regulating the use of artificial intelligence in nuclear arsenals as part of a broader global governance agenda.
The three countries had engaged in weeks of discussions to finalise the agenda and protocol for the talks, the report said.
Iran is another potential subject of discussion at the trilateral meeting. China is Iran’s largest trading partner and the biggest buyer of its crude oil, giving Beijing a significant economic stake in the conflict involving Tehran.
A senior US official said the war in Ukraine would not figure in the trilateral discussions, as Washington was pursuing a separate negotiating track with Moscow on the conflict.
China has maintained close economic ties with Russia since Moscow launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022. Bilateral trade has expanded despite Western sanctions against Moscow, with Beijing emerging as an important economic partner for Russia as it faces growing isolation from Western markets.
No bilateral meeting between Trump and Putin is scheduled, and Washington has no plans to engage with North Korea during the trip, according to the White House.
Trump will arrive in Shenzhen late on Wednesday for the two-day APEC summit.
He will also hold bilateral talks with Xi on Thursday. It will be their fourth meeting since Trump returned to office in 2025, according to the BBC. It will also be their third meeting this year.
Trump visited Beijing in May this year and held wide-ranging talks with Xi. He also hosted the Chinese president in Washington in September during a state visit.
Despite efforts by Trump and Xi to maintain stable relations through their meetings in Beijing and Washington this year, several major differences remain unresolved, including trade disputes, competition over artificial intelligence and tensions over Taiwan.
Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesperson Mao Ning said on Friday that China was in communication with the US and Russia on the proposed trilateral meeting.
Mao said the theme for the APEC summit is “Building an Asia-Pacific Community to Prosper Together”.
“We look forward to working with all parties to adopt the Shenzhen Declaration at next week’s APEC Economic Leaders’ Meeting, and achieve practical outcomes in areas that are vital for both regional and global economic growth, such as trade, connectivity, digital economy, and artificial intelligence,” she said.
The 21 APEC member economies are Australia, Brunei Darussalam, Canada, Chile, China, Hong Kong, Indonesia, Japan, South Korea, Malaysia, Mexico, New Zealand, Papua New Guinea, Peru, the Philippines, Russia, Singapore, Chinese Taipei, Thailand, the United States and Vietnam.
No South Asian economy, including India, is a member of APEC.
Shenzhen, located in China’s southern Guangdong province and bordering Hong Kong, has emerged as one of the country’s leading technology and manufacturing hubs. It was designated one of China’s first Special Economic Zones in 1980 and has since become a major centre of technological innovation and manufacturing.

sources.text:
Beijing/Washington: Chinese President Xi Jinping, US President Donald Trump and Russian President Vladimir Putin are set to hold an unprecedented trilateral meeting next week on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit in China’s Shenzhen city, the White House has said.
China is set to host the 33rd APEC Economic Leaders’ Meeting November 18-19, with leaders of the 21-member grouping attending the summit.
Discussions at the trilateral meeting are expected to focus on a range of global issues, including conflicts, artificial intelligence and nuclear arms reduction.
The proposed discussion on nuclear weapons comes amid concerns over the future of global arms control following the expiry of the New START treaty between the US and Russia in February.
The last remaining major bilateral nuclear arms control agreement between the two countries, it placed legally binding limits on their strategic nuclear arsenals. Its expiry has left the world’s two largest nuclear powers without such binding limits.
“The president has made it clear that, among other topics, he will discuss the reduction of nuclear weapons in the world, whose proliferation President Trump believes is very dangerous,” BBC quoted White House spokeswoman Olivia Wales as saying.
The Hong Kong-based South China Morning Post reported that the discussions could also explore possible commitments on regulating the use of artificial intelligence in nuclear arsenals as part of a broader global governance agenda.
The three countries had engaged in weeks of discussions to finalise the agenda and protocol for the talks, the report said.
Iran is another potential subject of discussion at the trilateral meeting. China is Iran’s largest trading partner and the biggest buyer of its crude oil, giving Beijing a significant economic stake in the conflict involving Tehran.
A senior US official said the war in Ukraine would not figure in the trilateral discussions, as Washington was pursuing a separate negotiating track with Moscow on the conflict.
China has maintained close economic ties with Russia since Moscow launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022. Bilateral trade has expanded despite Western sanctions against Moscow, with Beijing emerging as an important economic partner for Russia as it faces growing isolation from Western markets.
No bilateral meeting between Trump and Putin is scheduled, and Washington has no plans to engage with North Korea during the trip, according to the White House.
Trump will arrive in Shenzhen late on Wednesday for the two-day APEC summit.
He will also hold bilateral talks with Xi on Thursday. It will be their fourth meeting since Trump returned to office in 2025, according to the BBC. It will also be their third meeting this year.
Trump visited Beijing in May this year and held wide-ranging talks with Xi. He also hosted the Chinese president in Washington in September during a state visit.
Despite efforts by Trump and Xi to maintain stable relations through their meetings in Beijing and Washington this year, several major differences remain unresolved, including trade disputes, competition over artificial intelligence and tensions over Taiwan.
Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesperson Mao Ning said on Friday that China was in communication with the US and Russia on the proposed trilateral meeting.
Mao said the theme for the APEC summit is “Building an Asia-Pacific Community to Prosper Together”.
“We look forward to working with all parties to adopt the Shenzhen Declaration at next week’s APEC Economic Leaders’ Meeting, and achieve practical outcomes in areas that are vital for both regional and global economic growth, such as trade, connectivity, digital economy, and artificial intelligence,” she said.
The 21 APEC member economies are Australia, Brunei Darussalam, Canada, Chile, China, Hong Kong, Indonesia, Japan, South Korea, Malaysia, Mexico, New Zealand, Papua New Guinea, Peru, the Philippines, Russia, Singapore, Chinese Taipei, Thailand, the United States and Vietnam.
No South Asian economy, including India, is a member of APEC.
Shenzhen, located in China’s southern Guangdong province and bordering Hong Kong, has emerged as one of the country’s leading technology and manufacturing hubs. It was designated one of China’s first Special Economic Zones in 1980 and has since become a major centre of technological innovation and manufacturing.

"President Trump will conclude his visit to China with a trilateral meeting between the president of the United States, the president of the People's Republic of China, and the president of the Russian Federation," Wales said.
She said Trump's trip, which will also include attending an Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) summit in the Philippines on Tuesday, would "secure historic wins to the American people and advance America's interests in the Indo-Pacific".

Xi separately hosted both Putin and Trump in Beijing just days apart earlier this year, while the US president welcomed his Chinese counterpart to Washington in September.
Beijing has become a crucial trading partner for Moscow since it launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, which has isolated Russia and left it subject to Western sanctions.
But a US deal to import Russian diesel and the suspension of sanctions targeting the biggest buyers of Moscow's oil and gas - including China - heightened European concern about the Trump administration's softening towards the Kremlin last month.
Trump and Xi, meanwhile, have sought to project warmer ties at summits in Beijing and Washington this year - though little significant progress appeared to have been made on key issues such as trade, their race for AI dominance, and Taiwan.
The war in Iran has also been a sticking point, with Beijing the largest buyer of Tehran's oil and its biggest trade partner.

sources.text:
US President Donald Trump, Russian President Vladimir Putin and China’s Xi Jinping will hold the first three-way meeting between the leaders of the United States, Russia and China at a summit in Shenzhen next week, the White House said Friday.
Trump wants to talk about reducing nuclear arsenals at the trilateral talks on Thursday and is also set to bring up his war in Iran — but he is not expected to discuss Russia’s war in Ukraine, US officials said.
The three leaders will meet on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in the southern Chinese city, White House spokeswoman Olivia Wales told reporters.
“The president has made it clear that, among other topics, he will discuss the reduction of nuclear weapons in the world. This proliferation, President Trump believes, is very dangerous,” Wales said.
One of the major conflicts dominating Trump’s second term as president will feature, but the other will not, the US officials said.
“I think the president does intend to talk about Iran in the trilateral meeting with Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin,” a senior US official, speaking on condition of anonymity, told reporters on a call.
Washington has a “whole other track” of negotiations with Kyiv and Moscow aimed at ending the war in Ukraine, the official added, referring to talks that US envoys have had in recent days with Putin and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky.
“China is not really a part of that track, so it doesn’t seem appropriate to have the Ukraine discussion there,” the official added.
The meeting calls back to the 1945 Yalta summit in the Soviet Union, where then-US president Franklin D. Roosevelt, Britain’s Winston Churchill and Soviet leader Joseph Stalin laid out the post-WWII settlement and new territorial boundaries in Europe.
Zelensky has raised the alarm that the meeting in Shenzhen could be a Yalta-like “redistribution of spheres of influence” for the 21st century.
The Trump administration has sought to reassert US dominance over the “Western hemisphere” — including by capturing Venezuelan President Nicolas Maduro in January — but splitting the world among great powers like it’s 1945 may not guarantee security.
Trump will also hold a bilateral working lunch and meeting with the Chinese president on Thursday — their fourth meeting since the US president’s return to power last year. But Trump is not scheduled to have a separate one-on-one with Putin.
Among other topics, Nvidia chief executive Jensen Huang’s resignation over an affair with an alleged Chinese spy is not expected to come up in Trump’s meetings with Xi, the officials said.
“The situation with Nvidia should not really have any bearing on the trip,” a second US senior official said. The United States also did not plan to discuss export controls on sensitive chip technology, which were at the heart of the Nvidia scandal.
“We do not negotiate American export controls. These are national security matters that we develop in the administration… and we don’t expect it to figure at all in any of our conversations with the Chinese while we’re there,” the second official said.
Tesla and SpaceX boss Elon Musk will accompany Trump on his trip to China but will not be involved in the meeting with Xi and Putin, the officials said.
Trump will leave Washington on Monday and arrive in the Philippines on Tuesday for a summit of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) before heading to Shenzhen.

US President Donald Trump, Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin are scheduled to meet at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit in China in what would be an unprecedented group meeting, officials said.
The scheduled summit will unite the leaders of the three main global powers at a time of mounting geopolitical and regional rivalry.
This assembly serves as a message to the Kremlin, which can position Russia as a superpower alongside Washington and Beijing.
All three leaders joining a trilateral forum together would be another diplomatic win, with the opportunity to raise international security, trade and conflict issues impacting their interests.
The White House confirmed the plans Friday, saying the meeting was scheduled for Thursday in Shenzhen. Talks may deal with arms control and the war with Iran, but US officials do not expect an agreement soon.
Following the expiration of the New START pact between Moscow and Washington in February, Trump has suggested a new nuclear deal involving all three nations. But China has so far not been keen on putting together such a club.
But it could also trigger alarm bells in Ukraine, with President Volodymyr Zelenskyy worried about the great powers talking about the war without Kyiv, the Associated Press reported.
A gathering of the leaders was described as “important” by Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov, although he warned no specific design for the new world order should be reinforced.

sources.news_title: What will Trump, Xi and Putin discuss at their first-ever trilateral meeting?
sources.text:
US President Donald Trump is set to take part in the first-ever trilateral meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) Summit in Shenzhen next week.
The unprecedented gathering of leaders from the world's three biggest nuclear powers comes at a complicated juncture in relations among the three countries. According to media reports, nuclear disarmament and Iran are expected to top the agenda.
White House spokesperson Olivia Wales confirmed the planned meeting, saying Trump intended to discuss reducing nuclear weapons globally and describing nuclear proliferation as a dangerous development.
"The President has made it clear that, among other topics, he will discuss the reduction of nuclear weapons in the world. This proliferation, President Trump believes, is very dangerous," Wales was quoted as saying by CNN.
The last nuclear arms pact between Russia and the United States expired in February, removing caps on the two largest atomic arsenals for the first time in more than a half-century. Trump had rejected a call by Russia to extend the two-country deal for another year and called for "a new, improved and modernised" deal that includes China.
Although a concrete agreement is unlikely to emerge from the meeting, the engagement is being viewed as an opportunity to initiate discussions at the highest level.
According to a senior Trump administration official, the US President is expected to raise the issue of Iran with Xi and Putin but does not intend to discuss Russia's ongoing war in Ukraine during the trilateral engagement.
Before the trilateral meeting, Trump is also likely to hold bilateral talks with Xi, although no meeting with Putin is currently on the schedule.
Tesla chief Elon Musk is also expected to accompany Trump during parts of his China visit, with US officials citing his business interests in the country. However, he is not expected to attend the trilateral meeting, ABC News reported.
By agreeing to host the meeting, Xi may be calculating that the occasion offers an opportunity to showcase China's growing influence and international standing, according to an Associated Press report.
The report added that, for the Kremlin, the planned trilateral engagement represents a coveted opportunity to project Russia as a superpower on par with Washington and Beijing.

sources.news_title: Trump, Xi and Putin summit raises fears of a ‘Yalta 2.0’
sources.text:
A possible China-US-Russia summit has prompted alarm of a modern-day Yalta Conference, with three powerful men carving up the world — with little regard for Ukraine, Europe and Taiwan or anyone else.
But apart from an historic photo opportunity, the meeting between Presidents Xi Jinping, Donald Trump and Vladimir Putin at the November 18-19 APEC summit in Shenzhen will likely achieve little, analysts say.
Spheres of influence
When then US president Franklin D. Roosevelt, Britain’s Winston Churchill and Soviet leader Joseph Stalin met in Yalta in February 1945, they laid out the post-WWII settlement and new territorial boundaries in Europe.
That meeting in Yalta, then in the Soviet Union and now in a part of Ukraine annexed by Russia in 2014, laid out the foundations for the Soviet domination of Eastern Europe and the Cold War.
Ukraine’s President Volodymyr Zelensky has raised alarm that Shenzhen could be a Yalta-like “redistribution of spheres of influence” for the 21st century.
At talks in Abu Dhabi this week — the first since February — Russian negotiators rattled Ukraine and its European supporters by pushing a review of the continent’s security architecture as part of any peace deal, with the US also floating a new framework.
Russia’s delegation chief in Abu Dhabi, Vladimir Medinsky, fanned such fears by questioning the inclusion of Europe in further talks.
The trilateral rankles because it signals “the idea that a few great powers can decide the security and future of other countries over their heads”, according to Tsiporah Fried at the Hudson Institute.
The format alone “would already send a message about who counts, and whose interests can be negotiated by others”, she told AFP.
Divergent interests
Beyond the symbolism, however, divergent interests make the creation of a new world order in Shenzhen unlikely.
Even the agenda reportedly remains contentious: Russia has suggested the meeting focus on Ukraine, Trump has pushed for talks on nuclear weapons and the Iran war, and China has remained tight-lipped on both.
“The three parties have vastly different demands, making the management of expectations difficult. There is a high probability that talks could end without a breakthrough,” according to Wang Wen, dean of the Chongyang Institute for Financial Studies at Renmin University in Beijing.
There are also few issues where input from all three leaders could bring progress.
The main points of contention between Beijing and Washington are trade and the AI technology race, for instance.
Beijing — which presents itself as a champion of multilateralism — has repeatedly said that Europe should be part of peace negotiations over Ukraine.
German President Frank-Walter Steinmeier said that in a recent meeting, Xi showed “irritation” when the idea of the trilateral talks covering Ukraine came up.
“He explicitly pointed out that this is a European conflict, in which the Europeans must also be at the table,” Steinmeier told ARD.
On nuclear disarmament, China has long insisted that the US and Russia reduce their own giant nuclear arsenals before it agrees to talks on its own stockpile.
The summit therefore is more likely to produce minor outcomes such as crisis hotlines or some cooperation on counter-terrorism, public health, or climate change, Wang told AFP.
“There is no single enemy to unite all three great powers the way that the fight against Nazi Germany united Roosevelt, Churchill, and Stalin,” said Wen-Ti Sung, a political scientist at Australian National University.
“It follows that piecemeal horse-trading is in; a grand bargain is out.”
However, Taiwan — which China claims — will still be watching the meeting closely, Sung said.
“If the Trump administration is open to abandoning one partner (Ukraine) out of convenience, then it can abandon another,” he said.
A post-Shenzhen world
The Trump administration has sought to reassert US dominance over the “Western hemisphere” — including by capturing Venezuelan President Nicolas Maduro in January — but splitting the world among great powers like it’s 1945 may not guarantee security.
China has opposed the logic of Yalta — the clandestine division of spheres of influence and major powers determining the fate of other nations — “from the very beginning”, according to Renmin University’s Wang.
China could allay fears of a second Yalta by using the summit to “emphasise the defence of sovereignty and support for multilateral organisations”, Wang said.
If Beijing uses the meeting to insist on European inclusion in talks regarding the continent’s security, it “could, in fact, open a new window for communication between China and Europe”, he said.
“The original Yalta opened the path to the Korean War and Indochina Wars in addition to various conflicts and insurgencies across Asia, Africa, and Latin America,” said Chong Ja Ian at the National University of Singapore.
Any Yalta 2.0 agreement “will almost certainly run into the same kinds of issues”, Chong said.
AFP

Mr Trump plans to use the trilateral talks on Thursday to press for reductions in nuclear arsenals and is also expected to raise the war in Iran.

sources.news_title: Trump plans nuclear talks with Xi and Putin
sources.text:
Washington, Nov 14 (SocialNews.XYZ) US President Donald Trump plans to discuss reducing nuclear weapons with the leaders of China and Russia during an Asia visit next week, but US officials do not expect the three-way meeting to produce an agreement.
The meeting will conclude Trump's visit to China, White House Assistant Press Secretary Olivia Wales said during a briefing on his planned trip to the Philippines and China.
A senior US official described the planned talks as the beginning of a conversation about reducing nuclear arsenals, rather than negotiations expected to yield an immediate pact.
"We do not expect to get to any kind of agreement," the official said on condition of anonymity.
Trump intends to discuss Iran during the meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin, but Ukraine is not expected to be on the agenda, the official said. Discussions with Russia about Ukraine are proceeding separately.
No bilateral meeting between Trump and Putin is scheduled, although they will attend other events together, the official added.
The nuclear discussions form part of an itinerary combining regional diplomacy with efforts to implement existing trade arrangements. Wales said Trump would leave Washington early Monday and arrive in Manila on Tuesday evening, local time.
In the Philippines, he is scheduled to meet Quad leaders, sign a trade deal with Thailand and attend a US-ASEAN special summit. A state welcome ceremony, a bilateral meeting with the Philippine president and a banquet are planned for Wednesday.
Trump will then travel to Shenzhen for an APEC leaders' dinner. Meetings with APEC leaders and a bilateral meeting and working lunch with Xi are scheduled for Thursday, Wales said.
On trade, a senior US official said discussions with China would focus on implementing existing arrangements rather than announcing a new tariff agreement.
The official said US Trade Representative and Treasury officials had met Chinese counterparts through the Board of Trade earlier that day. Their discussions covered potential tariff changes and non-tariff barriers that could undermine the value of an agreement.
Washington remains dissatisfied with the pace and volume of Chinese shipments of rare earths and related products, the official said. That concern was part of the reason an arrangement referred to as the Busan agreement received a two-month extension rather than six months.
Trump is expected to raise the issue with Xi, the official said.
Any tariff changes would require separate legal procedures, including consideration of US statutory requirements and a possible notice-and-comment period, the official said. No announcement connected to the Board of Trade was expected during the leaders' meeting.
US officials also said American export controls were national security matters and were not being negotiated with China. Measures under consideration included extending licensing requirements to other countries to address alleged chip smuggling and examining restrictions on remote access.
Those measures remain under consideration, rather than announced policy changes.
Elon Musk is expected to accompany Trump for portions of the China visit, an official said, but will not participate in the bilateral meeting with Xi or the three-way talks with Xi and Putin. Those meetings will involve officials only.
The White House said the September meeting between Trump and Xi advanced work on bilateral boards of trade and investment.
APEC provides a forum for economic engagement across the Asia-Pacific. Wales said the administration sees its meetings as an opportunity to expand markets for American exports and advance its trade, energy and growth priorities.
